October 2026 FIRE Portfolio Update: Tech Is Smashed Again

  • ByJohnny
  • Last Updated On:November 4, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 14:31
Instaread

October 2026 was the beginning of a pronounced market correction driven by the same theme that has controlled the market for years, Tech and AI. After hitting all time highs at the beginning of the month, markets reversed course. Lofty expectations and earnings that didn’t live up to the hype caused the Nasdaq to enter correction territory. Much of this decline was market rotation as money flowed into healthcare and staples.

If you haven’t already read my posts before, I achieved Financial independence back in late 2020 with a portfolio of roughly $1.3m invested in mainly ETFs.

This post will be part of a monthly series of portfolio updates that summarizes how my portfolio performed, what trades I executed, what my monthly expenses were, and my general outlook on the economy/markets. This is by no means financial advice so do not look look at me for sage advice. I make stupid trades and make even worse losses quite frequently.

This is simply the performance of my portfolio and how it has performed on a month to month basis.

Monthly Highlights – October 2026

  • Net worth is at $3.2m as of September 2026 Month end
  • -$200k for the month
  • In October, we stayed in Bali the entire time
  • No travel plans for the foreseeable future

Market Moves

What is in my portfolio?

My portfolio is quite simple and straight forward. I have my holdings primarily spread out between a few ETFs, fixed income, and various single name stocks.

ETFs

Again, my primary holdings are in a few ETFs. My primary holdings are in VTI, VGT, and VCR. I’ve always been a big proponent of big tech and have been heavily invested in the Nasdaq for over a decade. This has paid off very well for me given the massive bull market of the 2010s and is essentially what allowed me to FIRE so quickly.

Read Also On My Blog:
January 2025 FIRE Portfolio Update: Trump Reign Begins

I used to hold more dividend generating stocks as I was really into this type of investing at a period of time. I currently do not have many dividend specific ETFs as I prefer growth more than income. This kind of goes against the ethos of financial independence but I have enough money coming in from other sources that I don’t need to focus so much on consistent income from my investments.

Single name stocks

Some of the single name stocks I own are the following

  • RDDT
  • ANET
  • GOOG
  • NBIS
  • RITM
  • MU
  • SNDK

These single name stocks make up less than 5% of my total portfolio. I tend to not buy much single name stocks anymore as there’s no point to take on unnecessary risks when I’m already so diversified with my ETFs.

Real Estate

I own real estate in Bali, Indonesia. While I’m not a big fan of real estate investment as an asset class, this is my personal home for my family. It’s hard to put a price tag on an amazing place to live that you can’t replicate in the rental market. As a home that my kids will make memories and grow up in, it’s no longer an asset that I need to profit from.

It’s hard to Mark to market the value of our home in Bali as the data is not so transparent. However, I believe that with the deal I was able to obtain, and the location of our villa, the value will at the very least hold on to what we paid for it. In addition, I took a margin loan against my portfolio to pay for the purchase. This means I didn’t sell any stock or incur any capital gains tax. I took a loan against my portfolio for the full amount of the purchase and pay an interest rate of 4.5% to Robinhood (my broker).

Fixed Income

I also purchased I-Bonds in 2022 at the height of inflation peak when I-Bonds were paying 9.5%. The rates have come down significantly since then as inflation itself has come down and I no longer bother with I-Bonds.

In the recent high interest rate environment, I had allocated a small portion of my portfolio to fixed income products, specifically purchasing treasury bills with 3-6 month expiry. These were paying out 5.5% which was a great guaranteed income generator. In recent months on the back of anticipated FED rate cuts, this rate was always going to come down which meant stocks should increase.

Read Also On My Blog:
September 2026 FIRE Portfolio Update: All Time Highs Again

Well the FED cut rates for the first time since COVID in Sep 2024 which means treasury bill returns will be decreasing for the foreseeable future. My last treasury bill expired in July 2024 and that cash was used to buy the market. I suspect I will not buy any fixed income products for the foreseeable future.

Market Commentary – October 2026

October was one of those months where the headline number hides most of the story. The S&P 500 only slipped 0.9%, which sounds like nothing. But it hit a record on October 6 and then finished the month about one penny above where it closed on May 29. So five months of drama, and basically nowhere to show for it.

The drama was mostly in tech. The AI worry that spooked everyone in July came roaring back. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.3%, its worst month since March 2025, and the Nasdaq-100 did worse, down 6.7% entering a correction territory as of early November. Earnings were generally good, but investors cared more about forward guidance and whether all that AI spending is sustainable. It didn’t help that the market had become so lopsided: the ten biggest companies made up about 41% of the S&P 500 going into the month, and AI-related industries roughly 53%. The month ended ugly, too. On Friday the 30th, the S&P fell 1.8% and the Nasdaq about 2.9%.

The interesting part is that most stocks had a great month. The equal-weight S&P 500 gained about 5%, beating the regular index by the widest margin since April 2009. Nine of the eleven sectors rose, led by energy, staples and utilities, and small caps rose 3.2%. If you hold a boring, diversified portfolio, October probably felt a lot better than the S&P headline suggested.

Then there’s oil and the war in Iran. Brent rose 13.6% in October, with WTI up 15.2%, as traders worried the conflict could escalate after the midterms and a tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz added to the nerves. The cushion is thinner than usual, too: the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has dropped to its lowest level since 1982. That feeds straight into inflation, which brings us to the Fed.

Read Also On My Blog:
The Ultimate Expense Splitting Spreadsheet

On October 28 the Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4% in a 10-2 vote, with two dissenters wanting a quarter-point hike. With September inflation at 3.7%, markets now expect a hike in December. Bond yields are the other half of the pressure: the 10-year closed back above 5% on the day of the meeting, and mortgage rates hit a three-year high of about 7.4% earlier in the month. When a risk-free 5% is on the table, investors get a lot less forgiving about expensive AI stocks.

What makes this a correction in sentiment rather than a collapse is that the underlying business results are strong. Blended Q3 earnings growth is running around 30%, with 82% of companies beating expectations. The S&P’s forward P/E is about 18.7, down from roughly 22 at the start of the year. Even after October, the S&P is still up more than 10% for the year, and semiconductors more than 50%.

Finally, the midterms, which are held in a few days. History says the run-up is usually the bumpy part: the S&P has averaged 2.9% in the 12 months before midterms versus 8.9% in all years, then 12.4% in the 12 months after. Going back to 1874, the index has risen in the year after 32 of the last 38 midterms. One more thing worth knowing: the midterm years 2018 and 2022 both had negative returns, but those sell-offs came from Fed rate hikes, not the elections. That’s a bit too close to this year’s setup for comfort, and the samples are small, so I wouldn’t read much into any of it.

Dems are favored to win and control both branches of Congress. Traditionally, markets have always favored most a split Congress as that means nothing gets done and the status quo of capitalism can run smoothly. Unified Republican control is a very close 2nd historically (unless it’s Trump who only cares about pumping markets and enriching his people) and then it’s much higher).

Market Value of Portfolio

Here is a history of my portfolio value. As you can see, it’s moved in line with the markets as should be the case since most of my holdings are in ETFs that track the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq.

In Sep 2025, I added my partner’s portfolio to the mix. I’ve avoided doing this for some time as this blog was mainly for my personal purposes but as we are a family now, it’s time to just aggregate everything for the blog purposes.

Trades executed for the month of October 2026

October was an passive trading month for me. The markets were whipsawing back and forth without much clear direction. Staying in Bali also means markets are open at night which does not produce good trading results. As a result, I mostly sold puts and bought the dips.

Portfolio withdrawals and expenses

Withdrawals from my portfolio is an important part of the financial independence ethos. The 4% withdrawal rate rule is one of the main concepts of the FIRE movement which I try to adhere to. Generally, I prefer to sell from my portfolio when markets are near or at all time highs to capture, and only when I actually need the cash.

For the month of October 2026, we stayed in Bali for the entire month without leaving. The lifestyle is just unmatched with so much emphasis on living healthy, eating well, and having social connections. With two young kids, having help is an absolute necessity and there is an abundance of nanny, maids, and daycares in Bali. I firmly believe that Bali is the absolute best place for me as a FIRE’d individual.

We have no travel plans coming up as it’s a challenge to travel with such small kids.

Expenses for October 2026

In October, our expenses finally normalized. We paid a lot of money in September for the gym and other startup costs so October was just the basics.

We did no traveling so our main expenses were eating out, massages, groceries, and other misc. expenses that you incur when having kids. We booked a business flight for a family member to visit Bali which was the only thing in the travel bucket. I also got a new tattoo which was roughly $500.

Overall, we were able to actually save money in October.

Historically, I was accrual accounting our expenses but I’ve decided going forward I will cash account all our expenses which is much more realistic as far actual financial management goes. A lot of our expenses in Bali are paid for upfront for multiple months. Things like rent are paid upfront as well as the gym (discount for paying multiple months upfront).

Earnings for the month

While the portfolio is the main source of financial security, we still have income coming from other sources. After all, if you can make money doing something you love, why not?

In our case, we have income coming from my blog which I will detail the numbers in the next section. My partner works part time at a travel related company and also brings in income to help with the monthly expenses.

My blog generates money every month to the tune of $5k or more and I cover exactly how I earn money from blogging in other posts.

My October 2026 Blog Earnings

I always give a run down on my monthly blogging income on these monthly portfolio reports because this is about my blog after all. My blog generates quite a lot of money from many years of hard work that it is a huge supplement to my FIRE portfolio.

My full 2025 blog earnings report has finally been released via my post in the links above. I made a total of $75k from blogging in 2025 which was an absolute monstrous and record year.

I earn money from blogging primarily from ads and sponsorships. My ads are managed by Mediavine which I joined in May 2024. In addition to Mediavine advertisements, I also earn money from Affiliate programs, sponsorships, and travel planning. More details on these things in my how to make money blogging posts.

In October, my blog traffic numbers continued to declined slightly as the spring and summer rush for travel content wanes. My Mediavine RPMs have increasingly stayed low as the overall ad market struggles I’m still debating moving from Mediavine to Raptive (another ad network) as they have been bombarding me with emails about how much who switch earn much higher RPMs. I don’t think it’s true but what do I have to lose?
